catalog_locator: Introduction 'The Äiwoo language', §1.1 Spelling, p. 2 (silent vowels + stress main rule); p. 5 (roots as distinct phonological words)
catalog_quote: No special indication is made of the so-called ‘silent vowels’. This term refers to the fact that, in some positions, the high vowels [i] and [u] are pronounced voicelessly (i.e. like a whisper) or dropped altogether. Simplifying somewhat, the rule is that these vowels are dropped in unstressed position (e.g. laki [ˈlakh] ‘be small’, nenu [ˈnenʷ] ‘coconut’), and that stress is shifted away from these vowels if there is a preceding syllable which can take stress (nubo [ˈnuᵐbo] ‘die’, but inubo [ˈinᵐbo] ‘he/she died’). It is not possible to drop vowels in consecutive syllables ... ngâgu [ˈŋɑᵑgʷ] ‘for me’, but ngâgumu [ŋɑˈᵑgumʷ] ‘for you’. Since the process of vowel devoicing or dropping is completely predictable, it is not indicated in the spelling. ... However, some vowels, most frequently a, tend to be lengthened in certain contexts. This occurs especially when they are stressed ... and…

audit.recode_to: Keep the segmental (high-vowel elision) and morphological (root-stress) perturbations, but restate the main rule as a right-edge moraic trochee: main stress on the syllable containing the penultimate mora, so a word-final long vowel or diphthong takes FINAL stress (nyenaa [ɲeˈnaː], nyikâu [ɲiˈkɑu]) while CVV.CV words are penult-stressed (teuwâ [ˈteu.wɑ]); set heavy = CVV (long vowel/diphthong; coda C also moraic per Viken) and what counts as heavy: accordingly instead of ''/not-applicable; add secondary stress on the head of each preceding bimoraic foot; cite Viken 2024 pp. 16-18 (reporting Næss in prep.) alongside Næss 2017 p. 2, and note that Næss 2017's 'penultimate syllable' is her own explicitly simplified formulation.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim at the stated places in the Næss 2017 PDF we hold (p. 2 §1.1 and p. 5). (2) Deciding source is a 2017 dictionary introduction by the principal fieldworker; Glottolog (41 refs, downloaded) lists no grammar or phonology for Äiwoo, and Næss's grammar is still 'in prep.', so among published works the dictionary is the best; Ross & Næss 2007 (downloaded from ANU) and Wurm 1969 PL A-21 p. 60 (downloaded) are silent/vague on stress position. (3) However a held-but-unused source, Viken 2024 (Oslo MA supervised by Næss), pp. 16-18, transmits the in-prep grammar's fuller analysis: quantity-sensitive moraic trochees built from the right edge, with final CVV stressed, plus the same high-vowel elision/stress-shift and root-stress facts our record already codes. That refines rather than overturns the record: the segmental and morphological perturba
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again:, confirmed in the copy we hold. lines 400-423 (printed p. 2, §1.1 Spelling; page footer '2' at line 433) carry verbatim the 'silent vowels' passage (laki [ˈlakh], nenu [ˈnenʷ], nubo/inubo, ngâgu/ngâgumu; one mis-encoded prenasal glyph U+0B86 in 'nubo' as B already noted) and 'As a main rule, stress in Äiwoo falls on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable of a word, but it is also to some extent tied to morphological structure, in that roots typically retain their individual stress in complex forms'; lines 565-576 (printed p. 5, §3 'What is a word?') carry 'kilolopâpäkomanato.

sources.quote: 'Stress in Äiwoo is based on morae. Each vowel and coda consonant constitutes one mora. Morae are grouped into feet consisting of two morae each. These feet are assigned from the right end of the word ... According to Næss (in prep.), stress is trochaic ... In a monomorphemic word, main stress falls on the leftmost mora of the final foot, and the secondary stress is assigned to the leftmost mora in each preceding foot.' Examples: päko [ˈpæ.ko], tememe [teˈme.me], nyenaa (ɲe)(naa) [ɲeˈnaː], nyikâu [ɲiˈkɑu], teuwâ (teu)(wɑ) [ˈteu.wɑ], nyiivä [ˈɲiː.ʋæ]; 'Roots maintain their stress in complex for

sources.quote: 'Vowel length appears to be phonemic, and long vowels are frequent. ... Vowel length and stress appear to be connected in many instances. Stress is predictable in most cases, and some of the apparent exceptions can be explained on historical grounds. A small number of as yet unexplainable instances remains - stress may still prove to be phonologically relevant.' No position rule is stated.
